claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by local chemical ordering and surface segregation.
A more uniform elemental distribution produces a higher melting-transition temperature than a segregated distribution.
A more uniform elemental distribution produces a sharper melting transition.
Greater surface segregation lowers the melting-onset temperature.
Greater surface segregation broadens the melting transition through heterogeneous phase formation.
As-synthesized solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles may contain chemically inhomogeneous regions and surface segregation.
Changing the synthesis route or cooling rate can control chemical uniformity relative to surface segregation.
Surface energy and atomic-level ordering significantly influence the transition in the premelting-to-melting regime.
Element-specific differences in surface energy drive variations in local chemical ordering during cooling.
Element-specific differences in diffusivity drive variations in local chemical ordering during cooling.
Surface segregation creates chemically distinct regions.
Chemically distinct segregated regions lower the effective energy barrier for melting.
Lowering the effective melting barrier lowers the melting transition.
Chemical heterogeneity broadens the melting transition.
A uniform chemical distribution maintains a higher and more abrupt melting transition.
Rapid quenching or optimized cooling enhances elemental uniformity in these nanoparticles.
Standard high-temperature synthesis with typical cooling rates produces some surface segregation and compositional inhomogeneity.
The proposed relationship applies to nanoscale Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particles under conditions where surface and interface effects dominate.
The proposed relationship may not extend to bulk materials or to processing conditions that cause complete phase separation.
Particle-size distribution, kinetics, and cooling-rate variation may affect the magnitude and breadth of the melting response.
